title: Holding history lightly
hookLine: pride and grievance both can weigh down

cards: Two backpacks. One is stuffed with trophies: the great libraries, the domes, the astronomers, the poets, the cities scholars crossed deserts to reach.
The other is stuffed with stones: the sieges, the conquests, the colonial years, the old wrongs nobody ever answered for. This year has handed out both bags.
Some people carry only the first, some only the second, and either one, carried long enough, bends the back. So what do you do with a history that heavy?

teach.h: THEIRS IS THAT WHICH THEY EARNED.
teach.b: First, a verse that can sound almost cold.

Speaking of the prophets and their families who came before, the Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Those are a people who have passed away. Theirs is that which they earned, and yours is that which ye earn. And ye will not be asked of what they used to do."

Some readers hear it as lifting a weight: nobody is credited with an earlier generation's glories, and nobody is charged with its sins. Each person's own account is the one that's open. Second, the trophies.

teach.h: THE NOBLEST: THE BEST IN CONDUCT.
teach.b: The Qur'an cuts pride in ancestry down to size: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct."
By that measure, a golden age is something to learn from and give thanks for, not a badge anyone inherits. Third, the stones.
Grievance can be just; real wrongs were done, and the Qur'an doesn't ask anyone to pretend otherwise.

teach.h: LET NOT HATRED BEND YOUR JUSTICE.
teach.b: But it also warns against letting old hatred bend present judgment. Pickthall again: "let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly. Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty."
The wrong is remembered; it just doesn't get to write the next sentence. Fourth, a picture from the seerah.

teach.h: MECCA: HE SET THE OLD SCORE DOWN.
teach.b: When the Prophet ﷺ entered Mecca, the city that had driven him out, the sources describe a general pardon for its people instead of a settling of scores.

teach.h: YOURS IS THAT WHICH YE EARN.
teach.b: He carried it, and he set it down. Lightly doesn't mean forgetting. It means carrying history in your hands, where you can look at it, instead of on your back, where it bends you.

how: Muslim teachers point to Qur'an 2:134 and 49:13 when warning against boasting about ancestors or living in old grievances, and to the Prophet's forgiveness at the opening of Mecca as a model of setting old scores down.

o: a single chapter of the Qur'an
the path believers walk each day
the story of the Prophet's life

games.q: holding history lightly — tap the pairs.
p: theirs is that which they earned
must not stop you dealing justly

s: the Qur'an says you will be asked about what earlier generations did
it says the opposite: ye will not be asked of what they used to do.
holding history lightly means forgetting old wrongs
it means remembering them without letting them bend present justice.
the Qur'an ranks nobility by conduct, not ancestry
the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct.

games.q: you return to the city that drove you out years ago, and now its people are at your mercy. what do you do?
o: forgive them and let them go.
leave the city without a word.
games.why: the sources describe the Prophet forgiving the people of Mecca when he entered it. the one with the most reason for grievance set it down.

practice: Find one old resentment: something done to you, to your family, or to people like you.
You don't have to decide it was fine; just hold it in your hands instead of on your back, name it as you breathe in, and let your hands open a little as you breathe out.
If you pray, you can ask Allah for justice where it's owed and lightness for your own heart; if you don't, simply notice whether the weight shifts.

wordCard.voice: Seerah, the biography of the Prophet's life, where Mecca's conquest is remembered for a pardon instead of a settling of scores. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: carry it lightly. Remembered, but not worn like a weight. Go gently.
